name: Chess.com
tagline: Online chess: rated games against humans, puzzles, lessons, engine game review, tournaments.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Everything technically hard about chess software is already free and open: Stockfish is stronger than any human, chess.js handles rules, and the Lichess puzzle database is public domain. So an agent can absolutely give you a board, an engine, puzzle drills and a move-by-move accuracy report in one session. What it cannot give you is a few million people awake right now who want a 10+0 rapid game at your exact rating, or the Elo number that means something because everyone else is on the same ladder. Paid Chess.com is mostly unlimited puzzles, lessons and analysis wrapped around that pool, and the pool is the product. Build the trainer, keep the account for opponents.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you play Stockfish at a chosen strength, drill rated puzzles from the Lichess database, and get an engine-annotated review of every finished game.
requirements: The free Lichess puzzle CSV (public domain) placed in /data
No accounts, no network calls at runtime
whatYouLose: Human opponents at your rating, on demand, at every time control
A rating that other people recognize and care about
Tournaments, arenas, clubs, friend lists, chat, spectating
Curated video lessons and structured courses
Mobile apps with cloud-synced progress and offline puzzle packs
Anti-cheat and fair-play enforcement, which is a large part of why rated games mean anything
moatNotes: The engine is a commodity and the rules are a solved problem. The liquid pool of rated humans across every time control, plus fifteen years of accounts and ratings people refuse to abandon, is not.
whyPeopleStillPay: Almost nobody pays Chess.com for software. They pay because the free tier caps the puzzles and analysis they use daily, and the reason they are there at all is that a rated game at their level starts in four seconds, any hour, with cheat detection running behind it. A local trainer covers the study half of the habit and honestly covers it well, but the emotional core of chess is beating a person, and that requires other people showing up.
notes: The trainer is a one-sitting build and it is genuinely good. The moat is the pool of humans who will play you right now and the shared rating ladder that makes the result mean something.
prompt:
Build a local-only chess training web app called "Pawnshop". No accounts, no backend server, no telemetry, no network calls at runtime.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite + React + TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, chess.js for rules and PGN, react-chessboard for the board, stockfish.wasm running in a Web Worker, Dexie (IndexedDB) for local storage. Everything ships from the local bundle.

Features, in scope:
1. Play vs engine. Choose Stockfish skill level 0-20 and a time control (unlimited, 10+0, 5+0, 3+2). Pick a color or random. Legal move highlighting, drag or click-to-move, promotion dialog, undo, resign, flip board, clock display.
2. Puzzle trainer. Read data/puzzles.csv (Lichess puzzle export: PuzzleId, FEN, Moves, Rating, Themes) on first run, load it into IndexedDB in batches, then serve puzzles near the user's local puzzle rating. Play the opponent moves automatically, validate the solution move by move, show the theme after solving, and update the local rating with a simple Glicko-lite or Elo update. Show a streak counter and a per-theme accuracy table.
3. Game review. After any finished game, run Stockfish at fixed depth over every position, compute centipawn loss per move, classify moves as best / good / inaccuracy / mistake / blunder, render an eval graph, and let the user step through moves with the engine's preferred line shown as an arrow.
4. Library. Save every finished game to IndexedDB with PGN, result and date. List, replay, delete, export PGN, import PGN.
5. Free analysis board: set up a position by FEN or by dragging pieces, get top 3 engine lines live.

Out of scope, do not build: online multiplayer, matchmaking, accounts, chat, video lessons, opening courses, leaderboards, mobile native apps.

Requirements: put the stockfish.wasm files in /public/engine and load them locally. If data/puzzles.csv is missing, show a clear one-screen setup notice telling the user where to download the free Lichess puzzle database and where to put the file. Any config goes in .env (there should be almost none). Include a README with setup steps, an npm run dev script, and one Vitest suite covering move legality, puzzle validation and the centipawn classification thresholds. Keep the UI dark, dense and keyboard-friendly: arrow keys to step through moves, space to flip.
